What this parcel is doing

Two years of satellite greenness, read in plain language - each point states what led to it.

  • Double-cropped, ~1.9 cycles/year. What led to this: the curve shows two complete green-up to harvest waves every year - a winter crop (Oct-May), then corn (Jun-Sep) - so the field touches bare soil (NDVI ~ 0.17) only briefly at each turnover.
  • 2024/25 winter was your half-wheat / half-berseem field - and the satellite caught the split. What led to this: during establishment the greenest half ran about 0.13 NDVI above the field average - the widest such gap in the whole record. That gap is two crops growing at different speeds on one parcel; your notes confirm it. Not a crop failure.
  • 2025/26 winter was berseem only - and its shape said so before you told me. What led to this: it peaked about 44 days later (March vs Feb), stayed green ~32 days longer, and carried the flat, multi-cut plateau clover gives.
  • Last year's corn (2025), left unsprayed for Fall Armyworm, looks normal in NDVI - clean, uniform, peak 0.81. What led to this: a 10 m greenness index cannot see FAW (it averages out patchy whorl damage, saturates near 0.8, and FAW hits yield/ears more than canopy green). See the corn section - a limitation, not a contradiction.
  • You're planting corn now (2026). What led to this: the record ends 19 June at berseem senescence (NDVI falling through 0.25), so this season sits just past the data's edge - the moment to start tracking it, ideally with a red-edge index this time.
  • No rice, confirmed both ways. You've never flooded, and the data agrees: MNDWI never rises above -0.30 all year - nowhere near standing-water values.

1 · Crop phenology timeline

Each rise-and-fall is one crop: green-up, peak vigour, harvest. Winter (wheat/berseem) tinted blue, summer (corn) amber.

How to read it: pale dots are raw satellite NDVI; the bold line is the cleaned, gap-filled curve. Each star is a crop at peak. Two peaks per year = winter + summer on the same field. With the record now starting 2 May 2024 it catches the tail of the previous winter crop senescing, a bare-soil trough in mid-May, then the full summer-2024 corn — so that corn now has its own green-up and planting estimate rather than being a partial cycle.

3 · Greenness vs canopy moisture

NDMI reads water in the canopy. When it falls while NDVI stays up, the crop is greening but drying - the earliest stress signal you get for free.

What led to the read: NDMI sits markedly lower through the summer corn than the winter crop - the corn canopy carries less water in the Delta heat, which is where to watch for irrigation stress.

4 · Year-over-year comparison

The same calendar laid over each year - did green-up shift earlier or later? Is peak vigour holding?

What the overlay shows: the winter peak moved later from 2025 (early Feb) to 2026 (March) - consistent with the switch from a wheat+berseem mix to berseem-only. Summer corn 2025 peaked later and higher than 2024. The autumn turnover trough sits in mid-to-late September both years - a stable replant window.

5 · Field uniformity

The gap between the field average and its greenest pixels. A wide gap = patchy emergence or a mixed stand.

The band is tight when corn is fully grown but widens through the 2024/25 winter - greenest pixels reached ~0.83 while the average lagged near 0.6. What led to it: you planted that field half wheat, half berseem, so the two halves greened up at different rates. The satellite was reading your split field, not a problem.

6 · Corn seasons & the Fall Armyworm question

You told me last year's corn was hit by Fall Armyworm because it went unsprayed. Here is the honest read.

What the data shows: last year's corn (2025) reads as a clean, uniform canopy peaking NDVI 0.80. So NDVI does not show the damage you saw on the ground - expected: FAW damage is patchy at the whorl scale and averages out over a 10 m pixel; NDVI saturates near 0.8; and FAW hits yield/ears more than canopy green. Update: the red-edge bands have since been added and NDRE computed (see §10) - it does not expose the damage at 20 m either, confirming FAW is a scouting / drone-scale problem with satellite as a backstop.

7 · Data quality

Phenology is only as trustworthy as the cloud screening under it.

32 of 280 scenes were dropped or down-weighted for cloud / low valid-pixel fraction before smoothing; cleaner scenes were given more weight inside the smoother.

8 · Inside the field — the raw pixels (bonus)

The delivered CSV is a field average. The raw Sentinel-2 cube keeps every 10 m pixel, so we can look inside this ~180 × 60 m field.

The field from space at each crop peak. At full canopy both winter crops look near-identical dark green (NDVI saturates), and summer corn is an even, lighter green. Grey / pale cells on the west edge are the field boundary (partial pixels).
Within-field winter structure = the berseem cutting pattern. The bright diagonal in the middle panel is not a wheat/berseem boundary (that clean split is not resolvable in a 6×18 image). It marks where NDVI swings most - the parts of the field worked hardest by repeated cutting. The control is the right panel: in summer 2025 corn the structure disappears (one uniform crop), confirming the winter pattern is real management, not noise. The next section shows the cut-front actually moving.
Two things the raw cube settled. (1) Validation - recomputing NDVI from the raw bands reproduces the delivered CSV closely (r = 0.94, near-zero bias, 232 dates). (2) The red-edge gap has since been closed - the cube was upgraded with B05/B06/B07/B8A at 20 m, so NDRE is now computed (see §10).

9 · Berseem cutting / fodder-harvest log

Berseem is cut repeatedly for animal feed; each cut drops NDVI, then it regrows - a saw-tooth.

What this shows. Each red arrow is a detected cut. The satellite cleanly resolves the synchronized early cuts (Nov-Jan); afterwards the curve plateaus because cutting becomes staggered across the field and averages out. Per-pixel the median is ~5 cuts for the 2025/26 berseem (on the clean, full-resolution cube) - right in the 4-6 range a Miskawi berseem really takes. Still a floor, since NDVI saturation and the 5-day revisit miss the shortest regrowth, but close to your true count.
The cut-front moving. Six consecutive scenes over five weeks: a freshly-cut strip (red/orange) appears in one part of the field and regrows while a new strip is cut elsewhere - the alternating, advancing harvest you described (cut a bit, move on, return once it has regrown). This is the spatial twin of the saw-tooth above; the faint persistent line through the middle is your central walkway (mamsha).

10 · Red-edge (NDRE) — now that the bands are in

You added the red-edge bands (B05/B06/B07/B8A, 20 m). NDRE is the chlorophyll-sensitive index they unlock - the one recommended for stress / Fall Armyworm. Here is the honest result.

What NDRE adds - and what it doesn't. At field scale NDRE moves almost in lockstep with NDVI (r = 0.99), so it does not reveal a hidden Fall Armyworm signal in the average - even red-edge, at 20 m, can't see patchy whorl damage. Its real value is the top panel: where NDVI saturates in the dense winter crop (~0.89), NDRE keeps headroom (~0.65), so it grades vigour and nitrogen in thick canopy that NDVI flattens on. On corn (bottom), 2025 - the FAW year - sits a touch below 2024 in both indices, consistent with the damage you reported but small and confounded by the partial 2024 record, so not a call to make from orbit alone. Bottom line: red-edge was worth adding (it strengthens dense-canopy and nitrogen work), but FAW stays a scouting / drone-scale problem.

11 · MSAVI vs NDVI (quick test)

MSAVI2 is a soil-adjusted greenness index from the same red/NIR bands. Does it beat NDVI for this field?

Same story, sharper floor. NDVI and MSAVI2 track almost identically over time (r = 0.98) - same cycles, same timing - so for phenology and planting detection they are interchangeable. The difference is at the edges: MSAVI strips the soil glow, so between-crop troughs read ~0.10-0.14 (genuinely bare) vs NDVI's ~0.25, and it saturates less (top panels: same field, NDVI 0.79 vs MSAVI 0.52 at the corn peak), spreading dense and moderate canopy further apart. Net: keep NDVI as the familiar backbone; reach for MSAVI specifically for bare-soil / fallow / planting-onset detection. It does not fix the real ceiling - still no Fall Armyworm.

12 · Cross-check — Hidden Markov Model (unsupervised)

Does an independent, threshold-free method find the same cycles? A 4-state Gaussian HMM (Baum-Welch + Viterbi) on the smoothed NDVI — no hand-set thresholds.

Current (threshold)HMM (unsupervised)
Method20% of amplitude + merge ruleBaum-Welch + Viterbi, 4 Gaussian states
Thresholdshand-setlearned from the data
Cycles found44 (+ a 6-day edge sliver)
Boundary agreement—~4 d at green-up, ~1 d at harvest
Per-day statenoyes, probabilistic
The two methods agree. The HMM learns four phenological states from the data alone — LOW (fallow), RISING, HIGH, DECLINING — and its activity windows land on the same four crop cycles, boundaries within a few days. A genuine cross-validation: an unsupervised probabilistic model with no 20%-amplitude rule independently reproduces the result, so the cycles are a property of the field, not an artefact of our threshold. HMM adds learned (not hand-tuned) thresholds and a per-day state probability (built-in uncertainty), and is well-cited for remote-sensing phenology; it needs a slope feature since RISING and DECLINING share the same NDVI level. The current approach keeps simplicity and directly-interpretable yield-proxy metrics. The lone 6-day sliver at the start is the previous winter crop's tail at the record edge, not a real extra cycle.

Method, in one paragraph

Field-mean indices from Sentinel-2 L2A were quality-filtered (valid_fraction ≥ 0.5), placed on a daily grid, and reconstructed with a weighted Whittaker smoother (lambda=3000) that gap-fills cloudy dates and denoises in one pass. Crop cycles came from multi-peak detection - deliberately not a single-season model - with explicit handling for partial crops at the record edges. Start/Harvest of season are where NDVI crosses 20% of each cycle's amplitude. The pixel-level maps were built by decoding the raw Zarr cube directly. Crop labels are your field notes; the curve shapes back them up. Nothing here replaces ground truth - it tells you where to look.
